why: chiselled angular stems, like temple carving translated into Latin
note: a Khmer-first family; the Latin is inscriptional with sharp triangular flares that function as wedge serifs, not true bracketed ones.

why: comic-shout caps, tightly packed and slightly tilted
note: comic-book ink lettering: angular joins that come to a point, with the stroke ends cut on a slant rather than rounded off.

condensed poster caps that go almost solid black at size
note: the 400 cut is already display-bold; tagged at its true colour rather than its nominal weight number.

why: hand-lettered market-sign wobble with flaring stem ends
note: stems widen at their ends without ever closing into serifs — that is the flared sans definition, and it separates it from the slab display faces around it.

why: dripping, spiked stems out of a monster-movie poster
note: the barbs at stroke ends read as sharpened wedge serifs; genuinely textured, so it earns a non-clean surface gene.

why: fat sign-painter script with ball-ended strokes
note: a connected brush script — the genome has no script gene, so it maps to the pen-derived humanist skeleton underneath, with the ball terminals carrying the script signal. The 400 cut already sets heavy, and the fat downstrokes against hairline joins put it above low contrast.

why: chamfered corners and squared bowls, reads like an instrument panel
note: variable wght 200–800; the listed statics are the useful cuts.

why: rounded strokes so thick the counters close to pinholes

note: ships only as an oblique — the slant is drawn in, not a separate italic.

why: near-circular bowls with clipped, tight apertures
note: listed as Display but it is a working headline grotesque with geometric bowls; variable wght 400–900.

why: inscriptional Roman caps with flared stems and a small x-height
note: humanist serif rather than wedge serif: the serifs are small but fully formed and calligraphically bracketed, closer to Trajan than to a chiselled wedge. The caps look broad, but the lowercase advances are normal — the small x-height is what reads as air.

why: sharp angled cuts and odd curve joins, retro-futurist

why: humanist mono whose ligatures fuse -> and => into single marks
note: monospaced; Fira Mono's humanist skeleton (open apertures, double-storey a and g) plus programming ligatures.

why: the Courier shape redrawn with real black, not the washed-out original

why: pointed-pen script with a bouncing baseline and swelling strokes
note: a script with no script gene available: the pen-derived skeleton is humanist, and the modulation is mild — downstrokes are only a little heavier than the joins, so it sits at low contrast, not the thick/thin of a copperplate.

why: quick ballpoint hand, monoline with long ascenders
note: disconnected monoline handwriting — no modulation at all, so it maps to the humanist sans skeleton rather than a pen-modulated one. Letters are drawn tall and tight; its advance widths are the narrowest in the set.

why: wet brush script, connected and rolling along the baseline
note: 1950s surf-brush lettering; near-monoline strokes with rounded ends, so the closest non-script skeleton is humanist sans.

why: thin felt-tip hand with letters that never quite sit on the line
note: monoline handwriting, so it tags as a humanist sans skeleton; the irregularity lives in the spacing and baseline, not in the outline surface.

why: casual signature script, strokes tapering to a point
note: pen-modulated signature script: strokes swell mid-curve and taper to a point at the ends, so the underlying skeleton is humanist rather than a flared stem-end face.
